title.text: Forests, boosting and overfitting: a stronger model without fooling ourselves

objects.text: How do we get a stronger model without fooling ourselves?

AI and Data Science Professional  |  Session 17 of 24  |  Module D: Machine learning
KLAi Professional Learning  |  Jotham Martin Wambi

slides.notes:
Welcome back. Last session we learned to judge a model with a confusion matrix, precision, recall and AUC, and to catch a column that leaks the answer. Today we ask how to build a stronger model without fooling ourselves. We start with a curve you can draw in Excel, then forests and boosting on the Nile Microfinance loans, then cross-validation to tune them.

The question at the end is a business one: when two models score about the same, which one do you ship?

slides.notes:
Here is what you can do by the end of today. You can explain overfitting and underfitting, and the bias-variance trade-off, by comparing training error with test error. You can describe how a random forest and gradient boosting each combine many trees into one ensemble, and tune their settings with cross-validation.

And you can read the coefficients of a logistic regression and the permutation importance of a forest without claiming more than they show, then choose the simpler model when the scores are close. We use the Nile Microfinance loans for all of it.

We have two hours. The first ten minutes bring back Session 16 and set the question for today. Then forty-five minutes of concepts, with no laptops open, so you can watch the pictures and the worked numbers. After a ten minute break we open the notebook for a forty-five minute lab on the Nile Microfinance loans.

You will predict each result, run it, read it, and change one thing. The last ten minutes are an exit check and what you keep. The lab is where the learning sticks, so please protect that time.

title.text: Three questions from last time

runs.text: 1.  A loan model scored far too well after one column was added. What kind of column does that, and what is it called?
2.  Why use 5-fold cross-validation instead of one train and test split?
3.  What does an AUC of 0.5 mean?

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_question_2.80.png

objects.text: Answer aloud first. Then we check together.

slides.notes:
Three quick questions from Session 16. Answer aloud first, and then we check together. It is a warm-up to bring last time back.

Question one. A loan model scored far too well after one column was added. What kind of column does that, and what is it called?

A good answer is this. A column that is only recorded after the outcome is known, here collection_calls. It is data leakage.

Question two. Why use 5-fold cross-validation instead of one train and test split?

A good answer is this. Each part of the data takes a turn as the test fold, so you get five scores and their average depends less on luck.

Question three. What does an AUC of 0.5 mean?

A good answer is this. The model ranks a defaulted loan above a repaid one no better than a coin toss.

If you missed one, check your notes from last session tonight. Now to today.

Here are the answers to the three warm-up questions. A column that is recorded only after the outcome is known, like collection calls, leaks the answer into the model. That is data leakage, and the score looks wonderful and means nothing. Cross-validation gives every part of the data a turn as the test fold, so you get five scores and their average depends less on luck.

And an AUC of zero point five means the model ranks a defaulted loan above a repaid one no better than a coin toss. Today we keep all three habits. Which one do you use already at work?

title.text: Words we use today

rows.text: Overfitting: the model fits noise, so training rows score well and new rows score worse. Underfitting: too simple to see the pattern.
Many small models combined into one. A forest averages trees (bagging). Boosting adds trees, each fitting the residual errors so far.
A setting chosen before training, such as max_depth. Parameters are learned from the data. Tuning tries combinations with cross-validation.
The drop in test score when one variable is shuffled. It shows what the model relies on. It does not show a cause.
When scores are close, ship the simpler model. It is easier to explain, check and maintain.

slides.notes:
Five words for today. I give the plain meaning of each, and we use every one of them before the end of the session.

Overfitting and underfitting. Overfitting: the model fits noise, so training rows score well and new rows score worse. Underfitting: too simple to see the pattern.

Ensemble (random forest, gradient boosting). Many small models combined into one. A forest averages trees (bagging). Boosting adds trees, each fitting the residual errors so far.

Hyperparameter. A setting chosen before training, such as max_depth. Parameters are learned from the data. Tuning tries combinations with cross-validation.

Permutation importance. The drop in test score when one variable is shuffled. It shows what the model relies on. It does not show a cause.

Parsimony (model selection). When scores are close, ship the simpler model. It is easier to explain, check and maintain.

title.text:
Underfitting, a good fit and overfitting
on 15 training weeks at the Jinja branch

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_ds_i_fitpanels_11.90x4.25_5eef055f.png
objects.alt: Underfitting, a good fit and overfitting on 15 training weeks at the Jinja branch

objects.text: Each dot is one week. Degree is the number of bends the red curve may have.

slides.notes:
Let us start with a picture you can draw in Excel. Each dot is one week at the Jinja branch of Lakeside Mart: footfall, the visitors counted at the door, against orders. We fitted a curve on only 15 of the 104 weeks, the filled dots, and kept 89 weeks hidden, the hollow dots.

In an Excel scatter chart this is a trendline: Linear is degree one, and the Polynomial option with order 2 to 6 gives higher degrees. Degree zero is an AVERAGE formula. Degree zero is a flat line at the mean, and it misses the pattern: that is underfitting.

Degree one is about right. Degree six follows the training dots closely but swings wildly between them: that is overfitting. The error is RMSE, the typical size of the miss in orders per week. Which panel would you trust to forecast next week?

title.text:
Training error keeps falling as the curve
gets more flexible, but test error rises again

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_ds_i_curves_7.70x4.80_f07061d7.png
objects.alt: Training error keeps falling as the curve gets more flexible, but test error rises again

objects.text: Training error always improves. Test error is the honest score.

runs.text: Test error: lowest at degrees 1 and 2 (6.9), then 17.4 at degree 6.
RMSE: the typical miss, in orders per week.

slides.notes:
Now the same experiment for degrees zero to six. The dark line is the training error, measured on the weeks the curve learned from. It only goes down, from 9.3 to 3.1. The red line is the test error, measured on weeks the curve never saw. It is lowest at degrees one and two, 6.9 orders per week, and then it climbs: 17.4 at degree six.

The chart stops there. Degree seven, which the Excel trendline menu cannot draw, has a test error of 82. So training error cannot tell you when to stop, because it rewards memorising. Only error on held-back rows can. Why would a very flexible curve do well on the weeks it has seen and badly on a new week?

title.text: The bias-variance trade-off: two ways to be wrong

objects.text: High bias: underfitting

runs.text: Bias is error from a model too simple for the pattern.
Wrong on training and new rows alike.

objects.text: High variance: overfitting

runs.text: Variance is how much the model changes when the training rows change.
Right on training rows, wrong on new rows.

objects.text: More flexibility lowers bias and raises variance. Pick the best test score.

slides.notes:
These two words come up in every machine learning interview. Bias is the error that comes from a model that is too simple for the pattern, like the flat line. It is wrong in the same way on the training rows and on new rows. Variance is how much the fitted model would change if you gave it a different set of training rows.

A model with high variance chases the noise of the particular rows it saw, so it is right on those and wrong on new ones. The bias-variance trade-off says you cannot lower both together by adding flexibility. You look for the setting where the test score is best.

Which of the two worries you more at your own work?

title.text:
A decision tree overfits as max_depth grows:
training AUC reaches 1.00 and test AUC falls

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_ds_i_curves_7.70x4.80_fd047b37.png
objects.alt: A decision tree overfits as max_depth grows: training AUC reaches 1.00 and test AUC falls

objects.text: max_depth: the most yes or no questions a loan can be asked.

runs.text: Gap = train AUC minus test AUC.

slides.notes:
Now the same idea on the Nile Microfinance loans, with a decision tree. The setting max_depth is the largest number of yes or no questions a loan can be asked on the way down. At depth three, training AUC is 0.738 and test AUC is 0.722. With no limit, the tree grows 31 questions deep and has 734 leaf nodes.

It scores a perfect 1.000 on the training loans, because it has memorised them, and only 0.583 on the test loans, which is barely better than a coin toss. The distance between the two scores is the generalisation gap. The tree here is our own NumPy copy of the scikit-learn algorithm, so rerun it in Colab before you quote the decimals.

Where does the gap start to open?

Each split question and its threshold

/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_tag_0.34.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_people_0.50.png

slides.notes:
This table separates two kinds of numbers. Parameters are learned from the training rows: the split questions in a tree, or the coefficients in a logistic regression. You never type them in. Hyperparameters are settings you choose before training. In a tree they are max depth and the minimum number of loans in a leaf.

In a forest or in boosting they are the number of trees, the number of variables tried at each split and the learning rate. You cannot learn a hyperparameter from the training rows, because the best training score always asks for more flexibility. So you choose it with cross-validation.

Which hyperparameter have you met before?

title.text:
Bagging: grow many trees on bootstrap
samples and average their predictions

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_ds_i_bootstrap_11.90x4.25_666201ff.png
objects.alt: Bagging: grow many trees on bootstrap samples and average their predictions

objects.text: Gold rows were drawn twice or more (x2, x3). About 37 percent are left out. Illustrative: 8 rows.

slides.notes:
A single tree is unstable, because a different set of training rows gives a different tree. Bagging fixes that by averaging. Bagging is short for bootstrap aggregation. A bootstrap sample draws rows at random with replacement, so some rows appear twice or more, shown in gold, and others are left out.

About thirty seven percent of the rows are left out of each sample. The picture uses eight made-up rows. We grow one tree on each sample and average their predictions into one. Each tree is a little wrong in its own way, and averaging cancels much of that.

Why would averaging help a model that has high variance?

title.text:
Averaging many trees lifts test AUC from
0.58 for one tree to 0.72 for a forest

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_ds_i_curves_7.70x4.80_cb8be78c.png
objects.alt: Averaging many trees lifts test AUC from 0.58 for one tree to 0.72 for a forest

objects.text: More trees help up to about 50. After that the curve is flat and small ups and downs are noise.

runs.text: One tree: test AUC 0.576 on average (0.547 to 0.615).

slides.notes:
Here is what averaging buys on the loans. One fully grown tree scores about 0.576 on the test loans on average, and the 100 trees range from 0.547 to 0.615. Average five trees and the test AUC is 0.656. Average a hundred and it is 0.719. After about fifty trees the curve is flat, and the small ups and downs after that are noise, so adding more trees costs time and gains little.

Notice that the training AUC of the forest is still 1.000. Each tree memorises its sample, yet the average generalises much better. These are NumPy forests that follow the textbook algorithm, so scikit-learn will give similar but not identical numbers. Why does the curve stop rising?

title.text:
A random forest is bagging plus a
random subset of variables at every split

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_flow_11.90x3.90_a7b9cf33.png
objects.alt: A random forest is bagging plus a random subset of variables at every split

objects.text: An ensemble is many models combined into one prediction. Test AUC on our loans: bagging with all 12 variables 0.709, random forest 0.719 (100 trees).

slides.notes:
A random forest is bagging with one extra idea. At every split, the tree may look at only a random subset of the variables, here three of the twelve. That stops every tree from asking the same strongest question first, so the trees differ more, and averaging different trees works better.

An ensemble is the general word: many models combined into one prediction. On our loans, plain bagging with all twelve variables gives a test AUC of 0.709, and the random forest gives 0.719. In scikit-learn the class is RandomForestClassifier. Its settings include n_estimators, the number of trees, and max_features, which is the square root of the number of variables by default, so three of twelve.

Plain bagging is BaggingClassifier. Which step makes the trees different from each other?

title.text:
Gradient boosting: each new tree fits the
residual errors of the ensemble so far

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_ds_i_boost_11.90x4.25_24736038.png
objects.alt: Gradient boosting: each new tree fits the residual errors of the ensemble so far

objects.text: Red line: prediction. Dashed: residual (actual minus predicted). Learning rate 0.5.

slides.notes:
Boosting grows trees one after another. Look at six Jinja weeks. We start with the mean, 36.5 orders, as the prediction for every week. The dashed lines are the residuals: actual minus predicted. The sum of the squared residuals is 287.5. Tree one is a single question about footfall.

It predicts the average residual on each side, and we add half of that correction, because the learning rate is one half. The sum falls to 219.4. Tree two fits the residuals that are left, and the sum falls again to 202.4. That is gradient boosting: each tree fits the residual errors of the ensemble so far.

What would happen if we kept adding trees for ever?

title.text: The arithmetic of one boosting step on six weeks

objects.text: Tree 1 asks: is footfall at most 1,638? The mean residual is +5.5 on the yes side and -2.75 on the no side. The learning rate 0.5 halves each correction.

slides.notes:
Here are the same numbers in a table, so you can check the arithmetic. The start is the mean, 36.5 orders. The residual is the actual orders minus that mean. Tree one asks one question: is footfall at most 1,638?

The two weeks on the yes side have an average residual of plus five point five, and the four weeks on the no side have minus two point seven five. We add half of each, because the learning rate is one half. That gives plus two point seven five and minus one point three seven five in the Tree 1 column.

The new residuals are smaller on the whole, and the sum of squares fell. Can you check one row yourself?

title.text: Forest or boosting: two ways to build an ensemble

objects.text: Random forest (bagging)

runs.text: Deep trees grow side by side on bootstrap samples.
Each tree overfits. Averaging cancels the noise.

objects.text: Gradient boosting

runs.text: Shallow trees grow in a sequence, each fitting the residual errors so far.

objects.text: Both are ensembles. Both need tuning, and both can overfit.

slides.notes:
Here is the contrast. A random forest grows deep trees side by side and averages them. Each tree overfits, and the average smooths that out. Its main settings are the number of trees, the depth and how many variables to try at each split. Gradient boosting grows shallow trees in a sequence, each fitting the residual errors of the ensemble so far, and adds a small correction each time.

Its main settings are the number of trees, the learning rate and the depth. Both are called ensembles, because many models make one prediction. Boosting is the more sensitive of the two, as the boosting curve will show. Which one would you try first on a new table?

title.text:
Boosting keeps improving the training
AUC, but the test AUC peaks near 45 trees

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_ds_i_curves_7.70x4.80_f3f9fc54.png
objects.alt: Boosting keeps improving the training AUC, but the test AUC peaks near 45 trees

objects.text: Past the peak, extra trees fit noise.

runs.text: Best test AUC 0.747, at 45 trees. Picked from the test curve, for illustration only.

slides.notes:
This is boosting on the loans, with learning rate zero point one and trees of depth three. The training AUC keeps climbing, from 0.763 at ten trees to 0.953 at five hundred. The test AUC rises to 0.747 at about 45 trees, then slowly falls to 0.720. After the peak, each new tree fits noise.

This is why the number of trees is a hyperparameter to tune. Picking the best number from the test curve, as I just did, is for illustration only: choose it with cross-validation. These numbers come from a NumPy copy of boosting that follows the same algorithm as scikit-learn.

What would you do to pick the number of trees without using the test rows?

title.text:
Hyperparameter tuning: grid search scores
every combination with 5-fold cross-validation

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_ds_i_grid_11.90x4.25_ebc1ddd5.png
objects.alt: Hyperparameter tuning: grid search scores every combination with 5-fold cross-validation

objects.text: 9 combinations × 5 folds = 45 fits. The best cell, refitted, scores 0.748 on the test rows.

slides.notes:
Grid search is the standard way to tune hyperparameters. In scikit-learn it is GridSearchCV. Here max depth is three, six or no limit, and the minimum loans in a leaf is one, ten or thirty: nine combinations. Each is scored with five-fold cross-validation on the training rows only, so the test rows stay hidden: forty five fits.

The best is no depth limit with thirty loans in a leaf, a mean of 0.746, with a spread of 0.007 between folds. 4 cells are within 0.005 of it, nearly a tie. Thirty is the largest leaf size tried, so a real project would also try 50 and 100.

The default forest scores 0.722 in the same cross-validation. Refit the best, score it once on the test rows, and you get 0.748. Why do we keep the test rows out of the search?

title.text:
Logistic regression models the log-odds of
default as a weighted sum of the variables

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_math_11.90x1.86_1dc13984.png
objects.alt: Logistic regression models the log-odds of default as a weighted sum of the variables

rows.text: Intercept and coefficients, learned from the training rows
The 12 variables, each scaled to mean 0 and standard deviation 1 (the 12 columns of Session 14)
instalment_to_income: loan x 1.15 / term in months / monthly income. The 1.15 is an illustrative assumption
z: the log-odds, ln(p / (1 - p)). p: the chance of default

slides.notes:
Logistic regression is the simple model we will beat, or fail to beat, today. It adds up the variables, each multiplied by its coefficient, plus an intercept. That sum is the log-odds of default. The sigmoid function turns the log-odds into a chance between zero and one. Take one test loan, the one whose predicted chance is closest to the median.

Its log-odds is -2.41, so the chance is one over one plus e to the power 2.41, which is 0.082, about 8 in a hundred. The coefficients are learned from the training rows, after scaling. The test AUC is 0.755. Session 15 shows 0.756 for the same model with 15 more indicator columns.

Why must the variables be on the same scale before we compare coefficients?

title.text:
Standardised coefficients: the instalment-to-income ratio
and previous late payments raise the log-odds of default

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_ds_i_hbars_7.70x4.80_c4bc511a.png
objects.alt: Standardised coefficients: the instalment-to-income ratio and previous late payments raise the log-odds of default

objects.text: Sign gives the direction. Length gives the size.

runs.text: instalment_to_income +0.80: odds of default x 2.2 per standard deviation.

slides.notes:
This is the readable part of logistic regression. Each bar is a coefficient after scaling, so a bar shows the change in log-odds for a one standard deviation rise in that variable, with the others held fixed. Red bars raise the risk of default and dark bars lower it.

The instalment-to-income ratio, the monthly instalment divided by monthly income with the illustrative 1.15 charge factor from Session 14, is the largest at plus 0.80. Raising e to that power gives 2.2, so one standard deviation of the ratio multiplies the odds of default by about that factor.

Late payments in the past raise the risk, and being in a group loan lowers it. These are associations in this table, and they do not prove causes. How would you explain the instalment-to-income bar to a credit committee?

title.text:
Permutation importance: shuffle one
variable and see how far the test AUC falls

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_ds_i_hbars_7.70x4.80_a3761637.png
objects.alt: Permutation importance: shuffle one variable and see how far the test AUC falls

objects.text: A variable the model relies on hurts the score when shuffled.

runs.text: Shuffle one test column, rescore, repeat 10 times. Pass scoring="roc_auc", or the drop is in accuracy.

slides.notes:
Permutation importance answers a question about a fitted model: which variables does it rely on?

Take the test rows, shuffle the values of one variable so they no longer match the loans, and score the model again. If the AUC falls a lot, the model was relying on that variable. We repeat the shuffle ten times and show the spread as the gold line.

For the tuned forest, shuffling the instalment-to-income ratio costs 0.061 of AUC, loan amount costs 0.022, and age costs about nothing. Notice that the instalment-to-income ratio and the loan amount are the variables a credit officer would expect. Does that match what you saw in the logistic coefficients?

title.text:
Permutation importance has
limits, and you must state them

objects.text: What it tells you

runs.text: Which variables this fitted model relies on, measured on test rows.

objects.text: What it cannot tell you

runs.text: Correlated variables share the credit. With a copy added, instalment_to_income fell from 0.061 to 0.021; the copy scored 0.030.

objects.text: Say: this model relies on the ratio. Avoid saying the ratio causes default.

slides.notes:
Permutation importance is useful and easy to over-read. It tells you which variables this fitted model relies on, measured on test rows. It cannot split credit between correlated variables. We tested that: we added a second copy of the instalment-to-income ratio. Its importance fell from 0.061 to 0.021, and the copy scored 0.030, because shuffling one copy leaves the other copy to carry the signal.

The credit was split. And a high importance never proves a cause. The sentence to use is: this model relies on the instalment-to-income ratio. Where in your own data do two variables carry the same information?

title.text:
Model selection: the scores are close,
so ship the simpler model (parsimony)

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_ds_i_models_7.70x4.80_3e32b7a4.png
objects.alt: Model selection: the scores are close, so ship the simpler model (parsimony)

objects.text: The top three scores differ by about 0.01, about as much as one fold differs from the next.

slides.notes:
Now we put four models side by side, all on the same loans. The black dot is the cross-validated AUC with one standard deviation either side, and the gold dot is the test AUC. Logistic regression scores 0.753 in cross-validation and 0.755 on the test rows. The tuned forest scores 0.746 and 0.748, and boosting 0.742 and 0.740.

The three differ by about one hundredth, and a single fold score moves by about one hundredth from one fold to the next, so we cannot say one of them is better. When scores are close, the rule is parsimony: ship the simpler model. A list of twelve coefficients is easier to explain, check and maintain than a hundred trees.

When would you accept a more complex model anyway?

Here is a decision to take as a group. A credit committee asks which model to ship. On the cross-validated and test scores, the three are close. Think about the committee: they must understand the model, a regulator or auditor may ask how it decides, and someone must maintain it.

My recommendation would be logistic regression, with the forest or boosting kept as a challenger, to be tested again if the data grows or the scores separate. But I want to hear yours. Tell your neighbour your choice and one reason, then one thing that would change your mind.

objects.text: In plain words

runs.text: Lines 1 and 2 fit a forest (100 trees by default).
Line 3: the predicted chance of default for each test loan.
Line 4 scores it. Score the training rows too, to see the gap.
The last lines try each max_depth with 5-fold cross-validation.

slides.notes:
Before the lab, read the recipe. Lines one and two create a random forest, a hundred trees by default, and fit it on the training rows. Lines three and four get the predicted chance of default for each test loan and score it with AUC. Do the same on the training rows, and the difference between the two scores is the generalisation gap.

Lines five to seven hand the forest to GridSearchCV with a dictionary of settings to try, and ask for five-fold cross-validation scored by AUC. After fitting, search dot best params underscore tells you the winning combination. In the lab you will run this and then shuffle the variables with permutation importance.

title.text: Five likely mistakes in the lab and how to fix them

rows.text: Forest training AUC about 1.00, test AUC about 0.72
That is correct. The forest memorises its training rows.
Write it down as the generalisation gap. Leave it as it is.
Build X from the 12 listed columns only.
ValueError: could not convert string to float
X still holds text columns such as district.
Select the 12 numeric columns by name.
Add n_jobs=-1 and run it once. Skip rerunning the cell.
Scores differ in the third decimal
Set random_state=42. Accept the ranges in the check table.

A value error about a string means a text column such as district is still in X. The grid search can take a few minutes because it fits forty five forests, so add n jobs minus one and run it once. title.text:
Exit check: three questions, then
compare with the short answers

rows.text: A model scores AUC 1.00 on the training rows and 0.58 on the test rows. What is happening, and what is the gap called?
Overfitting: it memorised the training rows. The difference is the generalisation gap.
How does gradient boosting differ from a random forest?
A forest averages deep trees grown side by side on bootstrap samples. Boosting adds shallow trees in a sequence, each fitting the residual errors so far.
Logistic regression scores 0.755 and a forest 0.748. Which do you ship?
The logistic regression: the scores are close, so choose the simpler model (parsimony), and say what would change your mind.
